questions.stem:
A particle $P$ of mass $0.25\,\mathrm{kg}$ is moving on a smooth horizontal surface under the action of a single force, $\mathbf{F}$ newtons.

At time $t$ seconds $(t \geqslant 0)$, the velocity $\mathbf{v}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ of $P$ is given by

$\mathbf{v} = (6\sin 3t)\mathbf{i} + (1+2\cos t)\mathbf{j}$

parts.label: a
parts.mark_scheme:
M1: Use of $\mathbf{a} = \dfrac{d\mathbf{v}}{dt}$: differentiate to obtain $\mathbf{a} = 18\cos 3t\,\mathbf{i} - 2\sin t\,\mathbf{j}$
M1: Use of $\mathbf{F} = m\mathbf{a}$: $\mathbf{F} = \frac{1}{4}\mathbf{a}$. Must be working in vectors
A1: $\mathbf{F} = \frac{9}{2}\cos 3t\,\mathbf{i} - \frac{1}{2}\sin t\,\mathbf{j}$ Or equivalent, e.g. as a column vector
Official notes (completeness pass):
- Differentiate to obtain $\mathbf{a} = \lambda\cos 3t\,\mathbf{i} + \mu\sin t\,\mathbf{j}$

parts.label: b
parts.text:
At time $t = 0$, the position vector of $P$ relative to a fixed point $O$ is $(4\mathbf{i} - \sqrt{3}\mathbf{j})\,\mathrm{m}$.

(b) Find the position vector of $P$ relative to $O$ when $P$ is first moving parallel to the vector $\mathbf{i}$.
(6)
parts.mark_scheme:
M1: Set $\mathbf{j}$ component of $\mathbf{v} = 0$ and solve for $t$: $2\cos t + 1 = 0$
A1: $\Rightarrow t = \frac{2\pi}{3}$. ISW if correct answer seen. Only answer $120°$ scores A0 here and the final A0
M1: Use of $\mathbf{v} = \dfrac{d\mathbf{r}}{dt}$: integrate $\mathbf{v}$ with respect to $t$ to obtain $\mathbf{r} = p\cos 3t\,\mathbf{i} + (t + q\sin t)\mathbf{j}\,(+\mathbf{C})$. Condone if there is no constant of integration.
M1: Correct use of boundary condition to find their $\mathbf{C}$. Could be part of a definite integral, e.g. $4\mathbf{i} - \sqrt{3}\mathbf{j} + \int_0^t 6\sin 3t\,\mathbf{i} + (1+2\cos t)\mathbf{j}\,dt$ for their upper limit
$\mathbf{r} = (-2\cos 3t + 6)\mathbf{i} + (t + 2\sin t - \sqrt{3})\mathbf{j}$
A1: one component correct; A1: both components correct: $= 4\mathbf{i} + \frac{2\pi}{3}\mathbf{j}$ (m). Accept $4\mathbf{i} + 2.1\mathbf{j}$ or better. ISW if they also offer $4\mathbf{i} + 120\mathbf{j}$. "correct" components after an M0 are fortuitous – A0
Official notes (completeness pass):
- $\left(\mathbf{r} = -2\cos 3t\,\mathbf{i} + (t + 2\sin t)\mathbf{j}(+\mathbf{C})\right)$
- $t = 0,\quad \mathbf{r} = (4\mathbf{i} - \sqrt{3}\mathbf{j})\,\mathrm{m}$

questions.stem:
A particle $P$ is projected from a fixed point $O$ on horizontal ground. The particle is projected with speed $u$ at an angle $\alpha$ above the horizontal. At the instant when the horizontal distance of $P$ from $O$ is $x$, the vertical distance of $P$ above the ground is $y$.
The motion of $P$ is modelled as that of a particle moving freely under gravity.

parts.label: a
parts.mark_scheme:
M1: Horizontal distance: correct use of suvat
A1: $x = u\cos\alpha\,t$ Correct equation
M1: Vertical distance: correct use of suvat
A1: $y = u\sin\alpha\,t - \frac{1}{2}gt^2$ Correct equation. Correct signs. Condone if not using "y"
dM1: $t = \dfrac{x}{u\cos\alpha} \Rightarrow y = u\sin\alpha\cdot\dfrac{x}{u\cos\alpha} - \dfrac{g}{2}\left(\dfrac{x}{u\cos\alpha}\right)^2$ ($= x\tan\alpha - \dfrac{gx^2}{2u^2}\sec^2\alpha$). Dependent on the first 2 M marks. Substitute for $t$ to obtain $y$ in terms of $x$ and $\alpha$
A1*: $y = x\tan\alpha - \dfrac{gx^2}{2u^2}(1+\tan^2\alpha)$ Obtain given answer from correct working (final step needs to be explained). Allow if $\sec^2\alpha$ seen. Must be "y" here

parts.label: b
parts.text:
A small ball is projected from the fixed point $O$ on horizontal ground. The ball is projected with speed $20\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ at angle $\theta°$ above the horizontal. A vertical pole $AB$, of height $2\,\mathrm{m}$, stands on the ground with $OA = 10\,\mathrm{m}$, as shown in Figure 3.

The ball is modelled as a particle moving freely under gravity and the pole is modelled as a rod.
The path of the ball lies in the vertical plane containing $O$, $A$ and $B$.

Using the model,

(b) find the range of values of $\theta$ for which the ball will pass over the pole.
(3)
parts.mark_scheme:
M1: $u=20, x=10, y>2 \Rightarrow 2 = 10\tan\theta - \dfrac{100g}{800}(1+\tan^2\theta)$ $\left(\dfrac{g}{8}\tan^2\theta - 10\tan\theta + \left(2+\dfrac{g}{8}\right)=0\right)$ Use given values to form quadratic in $\tan\theta$ or equivalent equation in one trig function. Allow working with $=, <$ or $>2$
A1: Critical values: $\theta° = 18.6°$ or $\theta° = 82.7°$. One correct value to 2 sf or better
A1: Range: $18.6 < \theta < 82.7$. Accept $\leqslant$ or $\leqslant$ $(19 \leqslant \theta \leqslant 82$ or $83)$ max 3 sf

parts.label: c
parts.text:
Given that $\theta = 40$ and that the ball first hits the ground at the point $C$

(c) find the speed of the ball at the instant it passes over the pole,
(5)
parts.mark_scheme:
M1: $y = 10\tan 40° - \dfrac{9.8\times 100}{2\times 400}(1+\tan^2 40°)$ Use given formula to find vertical height
A1: $y = 6.3(03...)$ (m) Can be implied by correctly substituted formula
dM1: Conservation of energy: $\frac{1}{2}mv^2 = \frac{1}{2}m\times 400 - mgy$ Dependent on the first M1. Need all 3 terms. Dimensionally correct. Condone sign errors.
A1ft: Correct unsimplified equation in $y$ or their $y$
A1: $v = 17$ $(16.6)$ $(\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}})$ 2sf or 3sf only

Alt: M1: $20\cos 40°\,t = 10$, $t = \dfrac{1}{2\cos 40°} = 0.653...$ Complete method using suvat to vertical component of speed e.g. by finding time taken then use of $v = u - gt$ or finding vertical distance and using suvat, then $\updownarrow v_V = 20\sin 40° - gt$
A1: $= 6.5$ $(6.459...)$ 6.5 or better (not final answer so allow >3sf or a correct unsimplified expression)
dM1: $v^2 = (v_H)^2 + (v_V)^2$ Correct use of Pythagoras. Dependent on preceding M mark
A1: $\leftrightarrow v_H = 20\cos 40° (= 15.3....)$ Horizontal component of speed seen or implied
A1: $v = 17$ $(16.6)$ $(\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}})$ 2sf or 3sf only

parts.label: d
parts.mark_scheme:
M1: $0 = x\tan 40° - \dfrac{9.8x^2}{800}(1+\tan^2 40°)$ Complete method to solve for $x$.
A1: $x = 40$ $(40.2)$ (m) 2sf or 3sf only

Alt1: M1: $y=0 \Rightarrow t = \dfrac{40\sin 40°}{g} (= 2.623...)$, $x = 20\cos 40°\times t$ Complete method to solve for $x$.
A1: $x = 40$ $(40.2)$ (m) 2sf or 3sf only

Alt2: M1: Range $= \dfrac{20^2\sin 80°}{g}$ Complete method to solve for $x$.
A1: $= 40$ $(40.2)$ (m) 2sf or 3sf only
